title: Acharei Mot: ask the person first (Mishnah Yoma 8:9)
hookLine: Yom Kippur atones between people and God, but wrongs between people need their forgiveness

cards: A sharp word at dinner. A man snaps at his brother, says something cruel. Later, alone, he sits quietly, sincerely sorry, and asks God to forgive him.
He feels lighter. Done. But his brother is still in the next room, still stung, and nobody has said a word to him.
Leviticus 16 promises that on Yom Kippur, the people will be cleansed of all their sins. All of them. The rabbis read that promise very closely, and found a condition hidden in two words.

teach.h: FROM ALL YOUR SINS, BEFORE THE LORD.
teach.b: Leviticus 16:30 says that on this day atonement will be made for you, from all your sins, before the Lord. In the Mishnah, Rabbi Elazar ben Azariah leans on those two words: before the Lord.
Wrongs between a person and God, he teaches, Yom Kippur atones for.
But wrongs between a person and another person, Yom Kippur does not atone for, until you make it right with them. Not even Yom Kippur skips that step. Maimonides spells out the steps.
Repay what you owe. Go to the person and ask their forgiveness.

If they refuse, come back with three friends and try again, up to three times. If they still refuse, you've done your part, and the burden passes to them. And he adds a word to the one being asked: don't be cruel.
When someone sincerely asks, forgive, even if it's hard. Because of this teaching, the days before Yom Kippur can fill with phone calls, emails, awkward conversations at the kiddush table.
People ask each other, plainly: if I've hurt you this year, I'm sorry, please forgive me. Yesterday's practice tore up a wrong and sent it away.
In the Mishnah's terms, that kind of turning belongs to what lies between a person and God. But if the wrong had a person on the other end, the order is clear.

how: In the days before Yom Kippur, many Jews ask family, friends and coworkers for forgiveness directly, and some recite a prayer of forgiving others, Tefillah Zakkah, before Kol Nidre.

o: after the death, the portion of the atonement day
the wrongs done between one person and another
the confession said over the goat's head

games.q: what's inside the teaching — tap the pairs.
p: make it right with them first

s: Yom Kippur atones for every wrong, whoever it hurt
the Mishnah says wrongs between people need the other person's forgiveness first.
Maimonides says to ask up to three times, with friends
after that, the burden passes to the one refusing.
the tradition tells the wronged person to hold out
Maimonides says not to be cruel: forgive when someone sincerely asks.

games.q: you've hurt a friend, and Yom Kippur is coming. what does the Mishnah say comes first?
o: fast, and the day will take care of it.
make it right with your friend.
games.why: between people, Yom Kippur doesn't atone until you've made it right with the person. ask them first.

practice: Think of one person you've wronged, recently or long ago, who has never heard you say sorry for it. Picture their face, and picture yourself saying it simply: I'm sorry for what I did, with no speech, no excuse, no but.
Notice whether that's hard, and stay with it a moment.

wordCard.voice: Acharei Mot. The portion of the Day of Atonement, and the Mishnah's teaching that wrongs between people need the other person's forgiveness first.

orig.note: Hebrew: "between a person and their fellow": the Mishnah's phrase for wrongs between people.

carryVoice: Your line: ask the person first. Some steps not even Yom Kippur skips. Day four hundred eight.
